Matched count regressions: Poisson, negative binomial, COM-Poisson, generalized Poisson, gamma-count, double Poisson, hyper-Poisson, exponentially weighted Poisson

Source: R/glm_families.R
count_reg.Rd

Fits a count regression with a log link from any of the package's count families, optionally zero-truncated and/or with unit fixed effects, returning an object that compare_models(), score(), dispersion_test(), dispersion_profile(), and the broom methods treat on the same footing as a cpb() or gec() fit. The families share one interface, so a gamma-count and a COM-Poisson can be compared to a CPB with identical degrees-of-freedom, log-likelihood, proper-score, weight, and robust-standard-error accounting rather than reconciled across packages.

Usage

count_reg(
  formula,
  data,
  family = c("poisson", "negbin", "compois", "mpcmp", "genpois", "gammacount",
    "doublepois", "hyperpois", "ewp3", "ewp2"),
  truncated = FALSE,
  fe = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  se = c("analytic", "robust", "cluster", "none"),
  cluster = NULL
)

Arguments

formula

A model formula.

data

A data frame.

family

One of "poisson", "negbin", "compois", "mpcmp", "genpois", "gammacount", "doublepois", "hyperpois", "ewp3", "ewp2" (see Families).

truncated

Logical; if TRUE, fit the zero-truncated form (requires all Y >= 1), the count analogue of the CPB's zero-truncated default.

fe

Optional column name(s) for fixed effects, entered as factor dummies (so the degrees of freedom count each absorbed intercept, matching cpb_fe()). Pass a vector of two columns for two-way (e.g. unit and time) fixed effects.

offset

Optional offset entered on the linear-predictor (log) scale – the log-mean for the mean-parameterized families, the log-rate (\(\log\lambda\)) for "compois". A numeric vector or the name of a column in data, e.g. \(\log(\text{exposure})\) so the model becomes a rate model.

weights

Optional frequency weights: a numeric vector or the name of a column in data. A weight of \(w_i\) is equivalent to \(w_i\) copies of row \(i\) in the log-likelihood, the information, and the score products, and nobs() returns the weight total. Survey (probability) weights call for se = "robust" or se = "cluster".

se

Standard errors: "analytic" (inverse information, default), "robust" (heteroskedasticity-consistent sandwich), "cluster" (cluster-robust; needs cluster), or "none". A robust or clustered covariance protects inference about the parameters of the best-fitting member of the family; the quantities that rest on the whole distribution (predicted probabilities, the mean of a truncated or two-part model) are still those of the fitted family. King and Roberts (2015) read a large gap between the robust and the model-based standard errors as evidence of a misspecification to fix; summary() reports their ratio. For the Poisson the coefficients are consistent for the conditional mean whenever \(E(Y \mid x) = \exp(x'\beta)\), whatever the distribution (Gourieroux, Monfort and Trognon 1984; Wooldridge 1999), and the robust or clustered errors are then valid for them: the gap shows that the variance is not the Poisson's, not that the mean is wrong. That makes the robust Poisson the benchmark for mean effects, against which the families' own mean effects (ame()) can be compared; a family that fits the distribution better estimates them consistently only if it is the true model.

cluster

Optional cluster identifier (a column name in data or a vector aligned to its rows) for se = "cluster"; supplying it selects se = "cluster" unless se is given explicitly.

Value

An object of class "count_reg". The component $theta holds the dispersion parameter on its natural scale (the negative-binomial size, the COM-Poisson \(\nu\), the generalized-Poisson \(\lambda\), the gamma-count \(\alpha\), the double-Poisson \(\theta\), the hyper-Poisson \(\gamma\), the EWP's \((\beta_1, \beta_2)\) or \(\beta\); NA for the Poisson); $fitted.values and $residuals are on the mean scale (the conditional mean E(Y | Y >= 1) for a zero-truncated fit), as fitted() and residuals() return them, and $mu is the family's natural parameter exp(offset + x'b).

Families

  • "poisson": the equidispersed baseline.

  • "negbin": negative binomial (overdispersion only); $theta is the size.

  • "compois": the classical Conway–Maxwell–Poisson in its rate parameterization, \(\log\lambda = x'\beta\). The rate \(\lambda\) is not the mean (though predict(type = "response") and fitted() return the mean); $theta is the dispersion \(\nu\) (\(\nu > 1\) underdispersed, \(\nu = 1\) Poisson, \(\nu < 1\) overdispersed).

  • "mpcmp": the COM-Poisson in Huang's (2017) mean parameterization, \(\log\mathrm{E}(Y) = x'\beta\), with the same dispersion \(\nu\); the coefficients are effects on the log mean and rate ratios are exact.

  • "genpois": the Consul–Jain generalized Poisson with constant dispersion \(\lambda \in (-1, 1)\) and \(\mu = \exp(x'\beta)\), the mean for \(\lambda \ge 0\), with \(\mathrm{Var}/\mathrm{Mean} = 1/(1-\lambda)^2\); \(\lambda < 0\) is underdispersion, on a finite support that the pmf is renormalized over, and the mean then departs from \(\mu\) where that support is short (small \(\mu\) at strong underdispersion: about \(1.19\mu\) at \(\lambda = -0.6\), \(\mu = 0.5\)); the exact mean is reported (see genpois-distribution).

  • "gammacount": Winkelmann's (1995) gamma-count renewal-process model, underdispersed when the waiting times between events are more regular than exponential (\(\alpha > 1\)); \(\exp(x'\beta)\) is the long-run event rate and the exact mean is reported (see gammacount-distribution).

  • "doublepois": Efron's (1986) double Poisson with the exact normalizing constant, \(\theta > 1\) underdispersed (see doublepois-distribution).

  • "hyperpois": the hyper-Poisson of Bardwell and Crow (1964) in the mean parameterization of Sáez-Castillo and Conde-Sánchez (2013), mean \(\mu = \exp(x'\beta)\), \(\gamma < 1\) underdispersed, with one \(\gamma\) for all observations: their constant-dispersion model hP\((\mu_i, \gamma)\). Their model with covariates in the dispersion, hP\((\mu_i, \gamma_i)\), is fit by DGLMExtPois::glm.hP(). Its underdispersion is bounded: as \(\gamma \to 0\) the variance falls only to \(\mu - 1\) for \(\mu \ge 1\) and \(\mu(1 - \mu)\) below, so Var/Mean is at least 0.5 at a mean of 2 and 0.9 at 10 (see hyperpois-distribution).

  • "ewp3" (alias "ewp"): the three-parameter exponentially weighted Poisson of Ridout and Besbeas (2004), a Poisson with centrality \(\lambda = \exp(x'\beta)\) reweighted by a two-sided exponential in the distance from it; $theta holds the two dispersion parameters \((\beta_1, \beta_2)\), one per tail, positive values underdispersed (see ewp-distribution). "ewp2" is its two-parameter form, \(\beta_1 = \beta_2 = \beta\). The coefficients are effects on the log centrality, not the log mean; the exact mean is reported.

The Poisson is the equidispersed member of every family, so dispersion_test() tests each family's dispersion parameter against it, and dispersion_profile() compares the families' implied variance-to-mean curves against the data.

Runtime: the Poisson, negative binomial, gamma-count, and double Poisson and generalized Poisson families fit in under a second at a few hundred rows; the COM-Poisson families, the hyper-Poisson and the EWP evaluate a normalizing sum per observation (and the mean parameterizations solve a root per observation), so they take seconds at a few hundred rows and minutes at several thousand. The EWP's sum lengthens with a heavy upper tail (a negative upper weight), and its standard errors sum over each observation's support. Rows that repeat (the same count, covariates and offset) are evaluated once with their total weight, so an intercept-only or few-category design costs as many evaluations as it has distinct rows. se = "robust" and "cluster" add numerical scores at the same cost per parameter.

Examples

set.seed(1); n <- 400; x <- rnorm(n)
y <- rgammacount(n, exp(1 + 0.5 * x), alpha = 2)     # regular event timing
d <- data.frame(y = y, x = x)
m <- count_reg(y ~ x, data = d, family = "gammacount")
m
#> Gamma-count count regression  
#> Call:  count_reg(formula = y ~ x, data = d, family = "gammacount")
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>      0.9847      0.4955 
#> 
#> Coefficients are on the log long-run rate scale, not the log mean; predict(type = 'response') and ame() are on the mean scale.
#> 
#> alpha (gamma-count dispersion; > 1 underdispersed): 1.9406  [Var/Mean ~ 0.515]
compare_models(poisson = count_reg(y ~ x, d, family = "poisson"), gammacount = m)
#>            df    logLik      AIC      BIC logscore       rps truncated
#> gammacount  3 -637.0878 1280.176 1292.150 1.592719 0.6721447     FALSE
#> poisson     2 -661.4718 1326.944 1334.927 1.653679 0.6905665     FALSE
#>            separated
#> gammacount     FALSE
#> poisson        FALSE
